figures.caption: Key visual. “A blueprint of meaning” — “It's more than just data.” On the ontology base sit semantic elements (dots and lines) and kinetic elements (approval and write-back).

figures.caption: Left: the blueprint of meaning (types, relations, constraints). Right: the instance graph built from that blueprint (also called a knowledge graph). Both, plus the moving parts (actions, functions, and dynamic security), sit inside one outline: what Foundry collectively calls the “Ontology.” The conclusion: the blueprint and the graph are different layers. A note adds that this is not a graph in the math-function sense.

figures.caption: The three building blocks of a decision: data (objects and links), logic (rules and models), and action (verbs, permissions, and write-back), each with a short form of the official question underneath. A pill notes that the architecture write-up adds security, as a fourth. A footnote says the premise is collaboration among operators, analysts, specialists, and AI.

figures.caption: Excel (you can attach meaning, but permissions, transactions, and side effects are not guaranteed to be controlled) versus an ontology of semantic elements plus kinetic elements, with “submission criteria (validation)” under the kinetic plate. The closer: meaning alone is not enough to control what an agent does.

figures.caption: An analogy from the show: closer to a “contract” than to “memory.” Memory easily becomes fuzzy; in contracts and internal rules, what's written is what counts. Above a set amount, a general manager must approve; higher still requires a board resolution.

figures.caption: On the left, ontology in the general sense is the blueprint layer (classes, relations, constraints; RDF, OWL, SHACL), drawn as one plate. On the right, Foundry is three plates inside one outline — “what Foundry collectively calls the ‘Ontology.’” From the bottom: blueprint (object types, link types, and properties), contents (objects and links), and moving parts (actions, functions, submission criteria, security, and write-back). A dotted line joins the two blueprint plates: “Same layer.”
figures.alt: On the left, ontology in the general sense is the blueprint layer (classes, relations, constraints; RDF, OWL, SHACL), drawn as one plate. On the right, Foundry is three plates inside one outline — “what Foundry collectively calls the ‘Ontology.’” From the bottom: blueprint (object types, link types, and properties), contents (objects and links), and moving parts (actions, functions, submission criteria, security, and write-back). A dotted line joins the two blueprint plates: “Same layer.”

figures.caption: Where each product draws the line called “ontology.” Left, Foundry Ontology: definitions, contents, and moving parts in one solid box. Right, the Fabric IQ ontology (preview): entities, relationships, and rules in a solid box, bound to existing data with no separate store. The graph sits outside the box, dashed, as an optional outer runtime that by default does not load instances.
figures.alt: Where each product draws the line called “ontology.” Left, Foundry Ontology: definitions, contents, and moving parts in one solid box. Right, the Fabric IQ ontology (preview): entities, relationships, and rules in a solid box, bound to existing data with no separate store.
